input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

[RID:web:paper:561567f6755c] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="arXiv" score=1.00 cite_key="2509.02949v1" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.02949v1" title="ProMQA-Assembly: Multimodal Procedural QA Dataset on Assembly"
Assistants on assembly tasks have a large potential to benefit humans from everyday tasks to industrial settings. However, no testbeds support application-oriented system evaluation in a practical setting, especially in assembly. To foster the development, we propose a new multimodal QA dataset on assembly activities. Our dataset, ProMQA-Assembly, consists of 391 QA pairs that require the multimodal understanding of human-activity recordings and their instruction manuals in an online-style manner. In the development, we adopt a semi-automated QA annotation approach, where LLMs generate candidates and humans verify them, as a cost-effective method, and further improve it by integrating fine-grained action labels to diversify question types. Furthermore, we create instruction task graphs for the target tasks of assembling toy vehicles. These newly created task graphs are used in our benchmarking experiment, as well as to facilitate the human verification process in the QA annotation. Utilizing our dataset, we benchmark models, including competitive proprietary multimodal models. Our results suggest great room for improvement for the current models. We believe our new evaluation dataset can contribute to the further development of procedural-activity assistants.

[RID:web:paper:194cc05ba640] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="arXiv" score=1.00 cite_key="2510.20303v1" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.20303v1" title="Citation Failure: Definition, Analysis and Efficient Mitigation"
Citations from LLM-based RAG systems are supposed to simplify response verification. However, this does not hold for citation failure, when a model generates a helpful response, but fails to cite complete evidence. In contrast to previous work, we propose to disentangle this from response failure, where the response itself is flawed, and citing complete evidence is impossible. To address citation failure, this work follows a two-step approach: (1) We study when citation failure occurs and (2) how it can be mitigated. For step 1, we extend prior work by investigating how the relation between response and evidence affects citation quality. We introduce CITECONTROL, a benchmark that systematically varies this relation to analyze failure modes. Experiments show that failures increase with relational complexity and suggest that combining citation methods could improve performance, motivating step 2. To improve LLM citation efficiently, we propose CITENTION, a framework integrating generative, attention-based, and retrieval-based methods. Results demonstrate substantial citation improvements on CITECONTROL and in transfer settings. We make our data and code publicly available.

[RID:web:paper:c618791d04a1] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="arXiv" score=1.00 cite_key="1802.05165v1" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.05165v1" title="Large-scale dynamic assembly of metal nanostructures in plasmofluidic field"
We discuss two aspects of the plasmofluidic assembly of plasmonic nanostructures at the metal fluid interface. First, we experimentally show how three and four spot evanescent wave excitation can lead to unconventional assembly of plasmonic nanoparticles at the metal fluid interface. We observed that the pattern of assembly was mainly governed by the plasmon interference pattern at the metal fluid interface, and further led to interesting dynamic effects within the assembly. The interference patterns were corroborated by 3D finite difference time domain simulations. Secondly, we show how anisotropic geometry, such as Ag nanowires, can be assembled and aligned in unstructured and structured plasmofluidic fields. We found that by structuring the metal-film, Ag nanowires can be aligned at the metal fluid interface with a single evanescent wave excitation, thus highlighting the prospect of assembling plasmonic circuits in a fluid. An interesting aspect of our method is that we obtain the assembly at locations away from the excitation points, thus leading to remote assembly of nanostructures. The results discussed herein may have implications in realizing a platform for reconfigurable plasmonic metamaterials, and a test-bed to understand the effect of plasmon interference on assembly of nanostructures in fluids.
input.section_draft:
Note on evidence grounding. General background knowledge: no external retrieval excerpts are available for this section, so the text below presents the authors' intended assembly, validation, logging, and mitigation procedures as a prescriptive system design rather than empirically verified claims. All procedure descriptions should be read as implementation specifications to be validated in follow-up experiments.

Assembly rules
- Input format. The assembly pipeline accepts as input the per-section JSON objects produced by the generation stage. Each JSON object is expected to conform to the project schema (required fields include: section_id, section_title, body_text, cited_evidence list, and metadata such as author_hint and generation_timestamp).
- Mapping to LaTeX. For each validated JSON section, the assembler maps section_title to a LaTeX \section (or \subsection) command and inserts body_text verbatim into the document body. Inline citation anchors in body_text must refer to normalized citation keys drawn from the cited_evidence list; the assembler replaces those anchors with LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{key}) according to the chosen bibliography style.
- Bibliography construction. The refs.bib file is constructed by extracting bibliographic metadata from each cited_evidence entry. For each unique evidence item, the assembler generates a BibTeX entry (entry type and required fields derived from the available metadata). Duplicate evidence items are de-duplicated by normalized identifiers (e.g., DOI, canonical URL, or an internal evidence ID) before writing refs.bib.
- Deterministic ordering and reproducibility. Section ordering is determined by the document graph scheduler (leaf-first ordering as described elsewhere); the assembler records the ordering and uses a deterministic traversal to ensure the same JSON inputs produce the same LaTeX output.

Conservative validation checks
- JSON schema validation. Before assembly, each section JSON object is strictly validated against the schema. Failure to satisfy required fields or type constraints is a hard error that prevents assembly of that section until corrected.
- Citation coverage check. The assembler performs a conservative coverage check that flags sentences or paragraph-level assertions lacking any cited_evidence anchors. Flagged units are annotated in a non-destructive way (e.g., comments or TODO markers in the LaTeX source) so they remain visible to human reviewers.
- Evidence metadata completeness. Each cited_evidence entry is checked for minimal bibliographic metadata (preferably a persistent identifier such as DOI or URL, title, and at least one author or year). Entries missing minimal metadata are flagged for manual curation and are not silently converted into incomplete BibTeX entries.
- Unsupported-claim detection (conservative heuristics). The pipeline applies conservative heuristics to detect potential unsupported claims, for example: sentences containing assertive verbs or numeric claims without an adjacent citation anchor. These heuristics are intended to prioritize precision (few false positives) over recall and therefore err on the side of surfacing possible issues rather than automatically removing text.
- Cross-section consistency checks. Using the document graph, the assembler runs simple consistency checks across dependent sections (e.g., ensuring that a claim marked as ``background fact'' in a leaf node is not contradicted by a later generated node). Detected contradictions are reported but not automatically resolved.

Logging, provenance, and audit artifacts
- Per-section machine-readable logs. For each assembled section the system emits a JSON log item containing: section_id, generation_timestamp, validation_status (pass/fail with error codes), list of cited_evidence identifiers, and the checksum of the assembled LaTeX fragment. These logs enable traceability from LaTeX output back to the generated JSON and the retrieval evidence identifiers.
- Global assembly manifest. The assembler produces a manifest file that lists the final section ordering, the mapping of evidence identifiers to BibTeX keys, and the versions of tools and template files used during assembly. The manifest is intended to support deterministic reconstitution of the manuscript.
- Human-facing annotations. When conservative checks flag issues, the assembler inserts clear, reviewable annotations in the LaTeX (and optionally generates a companion HTML report) so editors can rapidly identify and fix problematic sections.

Documented failure modes and remediation steps
- Missing or incomplete evidence metadata. Symptom: refs.bib lacks entries for one or more citation anchors or entries are incomplete. Remediation: prompt retrieval re-run for the affected evidence identifiers; if persistent, flag for manual bibliographic curation and suspend assembly of the dependent sections.
- Invalid JSON output. Symptom: section JSON fails schema validation. Remediation: provide the validation error to the generation module and either (a) re-run constrained generation for the section, or (b) allow a human editor to correct the JSON in a guided interface.
- Citation-anchor mismatch. Symptom: inline anchors in body_text do not match any cited_evidence keys. Remediation: run an automated anchor-key reconciliation pass that attempts to match by normalized titles or DOIs; if unresolved, mark anchors and require human review.
- Hallucinated or unsupported assertions. Symptom: conservative unsupported-claim detector flags assertions lacking evidence. Remediation: attempt an automated evidence retrieval for the flagged assertions; if no high-confidence evidence is found, leave conspicuous TODO annotations and defer to human authors for either insertion of evidence or removal/rephrasing of the claim.
- Contradictions across sections. Symptom: cross-section check identifies contradictory statements between dependent nodes. Remediation: surface both claims in a conflict report tied to the document graph edges; suggest re-generation of the later node under stronger constraints or require human adjudication.

Practical safeguards and integration with human workflows
- Fail-fast, human-in-the-loop. The assembler is designed to fail fast on hard errors (schema violations, missing minimal bibliographic metadata) while using conservative automated checks to surface softer issues for human review.
- Auditability. Machine-readable logs, the assembly manifest, and annotated LaTeX together provide the minimal provenance artifacts required for post-hoc audits and partial rollbacks of assembled manuscripts.
- Documentation and remediation templates. For each class of failure the system emits a remediation template that advises authors or editors on low-effort corrective actions (e.g., exact retrieval query strings to find missing metadata, or a prompt template to regenerate a section with a stronger citation constraint).

Limitations and next steps (brief)
- General background knowledge: the procedures above are design specifications that require empirical validation. Future work will quantify the effectiveness of these checks and the human effort required for remediation under realistic generation error distributions.

- JSON schema validation. Before assembly, each section JSON object is strictly validated against the schema. Schema violations (missing required fields, incorrect types, malformed citation lists) are treated as hard errors that block assembly of the affected section and are surfaced to the generation module or a human editor for correction.

- Citation coverage check. The assembler performs a conservative coverage check that flags sentences or paragraph‑level assertions that do not contain any cited_evidence anchors. The heuristics are designed to prioritize precision (minimizing false positives) over recall so that the system surfaces likely problems rather than automatically removing or altering content. This design choice is motivated by prior analyses that disentangle citation failure (absence or incompleteness of citations) from response failure (flaws in the substantive content) and that emphasize combining detection and mitigation strategies for citation reliability \cite{2510.20303v1}.

- Cross‑section consistency checks. Leveraging the document graph, the assembler runs deterministic consistency checks across dependent sections (for example, verifying that a background fact asserted in a leaf node is not contradicted by a dependent node). Detected contradictions are reported in a conflict log but are not automatically reconciled; the report identifies the graph edges implicated in each inconsistency to guide targeted regeneration or human adjudication.

Logging, provenance, and audit artifacts

- Per‑section machine‑readable logs. For each assembled section the system emits a JSON log record that contains section_id, generation_timestamp, validation_status (pass/fail with standardized error codes), list of cited_evidence identifiers, and a checksum of the assembled LaTeX fragment. These per‑section records enable traceability from the final manuscript back to the original generated JSON and to the retrieval evidence identifiers.

- Global assembly manifest. The assembler produces a manifest file that enumerates the final section ordering, the mapping of evidence identifiers to BibTeX keys, and versions of tools, templates, and retrieval indexes used during assembly. The manifest is intended to support deterministic reconstitution of the manuscript and reproducible auditing.

- Human‑facing annotations and reports. When conservative checks flag issues, the assembler inserts clear, reviewable annotations into the LaTeX source and optionally generates a companion HTML report that aggregates flagged items by severity, section, and error code. The report links each flag to the corresponding per‑section log entry and to the evidence identifiers that were available at generation time.

Documented failure modes and remediation steps

- Missing or incomplete evidence metadata. Symptom: refs.bib lacks entries for one or more citation anchors or contains incomplete entries. Remediation: re‑run retrieval for the affected evidence identifiers with stricter query formulations; if automated retrieval fails to yield persistent identifiers, flag the evidence for manual bibliographic curation and suspend assembly of dependent sections until curation is complete.

- Invalid JSON output. Symptom: section JSON fails schema validation. Remediation: return structured validation errors to the generation module and either (a) re‑run constrained generation for the section with the appropriate schema and error context, or (b) allow a human editor to correct the JSON via a guided interface that enforces schema constraints.

- Citation‑anchor mismatch. Symptom: inline anchors in body_text do not match any cited_evidence keys. Remediation: perform an automated reconciliation pass that attempts to match anchors to evidence entries by normalized title, DOI, or URL; unresolved anchors are annotated for human review and inerted so that they do not produce broken citations in the final build.

- Hallucinated or unsupported assertions. Symptom: the unsupported‑claim detector flags assertions that lack high‑confidence supporting evidence. Remediation: attempt automated retrieval for the flagged assertions using focused queries; if no high‑confidence matches are found, insert conspicuous TODO annotations and require human authors to either supply evidence, rephrase the claim to a supported statement, or remove it. The pipeline explicitly treats such cases as human‑in‑the‑loop decisions rather than automatic deletions.

- Contradictions across sections. Symptom: cross‑section checks identify contradictory statements between dependent nodes. Remediation: surface both claims in a conflict report tied to the document graph edges; recommend regenerating the later node under stronger evidence constraints or require human adjudication. The conflict report includes the supporting evidence lists for each claim to aid rapid resolution.

Practical safeguards and integration with human workflows

- Fail‑fast, human‑in‑the‑loop. The assembler is designed to fail fast on hard errors (schema violations, missing minimal bibliographic metadata) while using conservative automated checks to surface softer issues for human review. This strategy reduces the risk of silent errors propagating into the published artifact.

- Auditability. Machine‑readable logs, the assembly manifest, and annotated LaTeX together provide the provenance artifacts necessary for post‑hoc audits and for partial rollbacks of assembled manuscripts. These artifacts are intended to enable reproducible investigation of any claim in the final document back to generation and retrieval steps.

- Documentation and remediation templates. For each failure class the system emits a remediation template that advises editors on low‑effort corrective actions (for example, precise retrieval query strings to locate missing metadata or a constrained prompt template to regenerate a section with a stronger citation requirement).

Limitations and next steps

- General background knowledge: the procedures described above are design specifications and require empirical validation. In particular, the effectiveness of conservative checks, the human effort required for remediation, and the impact of assembly‑level safeguards on final manuscript quality remain to be quantified in controlled experiments. Future work will instrument user studies and error‑distribution analyses to measure these quantities and to refine the assembler and its remediation workflows.
